# Results — Study 204 (Talmud-Portfolio) on real daily data

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Three ETFs —
VNQ (real estate / "land"), SPY (stocks / "business"), BND (bonds / "reserve") —
rebalanced annually at 10 bps one-way rebalance cost. Compared to 60/40 (SPY/BND),
100% SPY, and 50/50 SPY/VNQ. Sharpe computed on excess-of-BND returns. As-of
**2026-06-15**.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Role in Talmud | Window | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| VNQ | Land (real estate) | 2007-04-10 -> 2026-06-11 | `520e262c08ac` |
| SPY | Business (stocks) | 2007-04-10 -> 2026-06-11 | `520e262c08ac` |
| BND | Reserve (bonds/cash) | 2007-04-10 -> 2026-06-11 | `520e262c08ac` |

Combined fingerprint: **`520e262c08ac`** — n = 4,825 trading days (~19.1 years).

## Headline stats (10 bps one-way rebalance cost, excess-of-BND Sharpe)

| Portfolio | CAGR | Sharpe | Vol | Max DD | Worst Year |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Talmud 1/3–1/3–1/3** | **6.9%** | **+0.31** | **14.6%** | **-44.0%** | **-22.3%** |
| 60/40 (SPY/BND) | 8.1% | +0.46 | 11.5% | -33.8% | -19.3% |
| SPY 100% | 10.9% | +0.45 | 19.7% | -55.2% | -36.8% |
| SPY/VNQ 50/50 | 8.3% | +0.32 | 22.9% | -62.6% | -36.9% |

The Talmud blend delivers **lower CAGR**, **lower Sharpe**, and **deeper max drawdown**
than the 60/40 benchmark on every metric. Its only advantage is versus 100% SPY on
volatility and worst-year loss — which 60/40 already provides more efficiently.

## HAC t-stats on annual return differences (Talmud vs benchmark)

| Comparison | Annual mean diff | HAC t-stat | Verdict |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| Talmud vs 60/40 (SPY/BND) | -1.2 pp/yr | **-1.26** | Not significant (weakly negative) |
| Talmud vs SPY 100% | -4.0 pp/yr | **-3.03** | Significant — Talmud *trails* SPY |
| Talmud vs SPY/VNQ 50/50 | +0.4 pp/yr | **-1.95** | Not significant |

- n = 19 annual observations (2007–2025 inclusive).
- The Talmud blend does **not** outperform 60/40 at any conventional significance threshold.
- It significantly underperforms 100% SPY — but that is expected for a diversified portfolio.
- Adding a REIT leg offers no statistically detectable improvement over 60/40.

## Why the REIT leg hurts — crash behaviour

The critical flaw: VNQ (REITs) is **highly correlated with stocks in crises** and
therefore amplifies — not hedges — equity crashes. Every major crash in the sample shows
VNQ falling as much as, or more than, SPY:

| Crash episode | SPY | VNQ | BND |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| GFC (Oct 2007 – Mar 2009) | -55.2% | **-69.3%** | +7.5% |
| Q4 2018 | -19.3% | -11.1% | +1.3% |
| COVID crash (Feb–Mar 2020) | -33.7% | **-41.5%** | -1.4% |
| 2022 rate shock | -24.5% | **-31.9%** | -14.5% |
| Tariff shock (Feb–Apr 2025) | -18.8% | -12.5% | +0.8% |

BND provides the genuine hedge (positive or flat in 4 of 5 episodes); VNQ provides no
defensive cushion and in the two largest crashes it fell *harder* than SPY. Replacing
40% of the 60/40 bond leg with REITs thus removes the actual hedge and adds correlated
crash risk — the opposite of the Talmud's diversification intent.

The Talmud outperforms 60/40 in years when REITs boom (2010, 2014, 2019, 2021) but
trails badly in bond-heavy years (2013, 2020, 2024) and crashes (2008, 2022).
The mean deficit of -1.2 pp/yr vs 60/40 is not statistically significant but consistently
negative over the 19-year sample.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The Talmud allocation delivers a real (positive) Sharpe ratio and
  diversification benefit vs 100% stocks. But it does NOT outperform the simpler 60/40
  benchmark (HAC t = -1.26, not significant), and the REIT leg demonstrably fails its
  diversification role in major crashes. The "effect" is that of any diversified portfolio
  relative to 100% stocks — not a distinct 2,000-year-old insight.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The blend is tradable (low turnover, liquid ETFs, low costs),
  but it is dominated by 60/40 on every risk-adjusted metric. An investor who followed
  this allocation forfeited ~1.2 pp/yr vs 60/40 over 19 years with higher drawdowns —
  the ancient wisdom adds no practical value over the well-known modern alternative.
- **vs 60/40? — No edge.** The Talmud's distinctiveness — adding real estate — is
  exactly the element that hurts it. Bonds hedge; REITs amplify. The 2,000-year-old
  three-way split is a reasonable diversified allocation but an inferior one to a
  modern risk-balanced 60/40.
